Yeah, Max, I've been thinking about how to put it all together. I'm excited about letting my friends and family see all the stuff I've produced. Me too. Actually, I'm really keen to see the work of the other students on our course. I mean, it'll be great to see all the finished displays. But we've seen what they've been doing throughout the year already, really. Anyway, what about getting feedback on our exhibition from our tutor? I wonder what that'll be like. I'm a bit nervous about that part. I hope our stuff ends up looking as good as some of the displays in last year's exhibition. Yeah! Do you remember that display of printed textiles? Fantastic mixtures of silk and wool, all colored with natural dyes. Yeah, I can't actually remember that. What sticks in my mind are those ten wooden reproductions one student made, all of different types of transport, little cars and trains and stuff. Yes, it was really delicate work and much harder to do than if he'd tried to construct them out of metal. So our tutor asked us to come up with a name for our display which reflects the work we've done. What have you gone for? Well, most of what I've done has focused on the countryside, so I've been thinking of things connected to that. A lot of my larger pieces are views of farmland. That's not a particularly memorable name though. I've gone for ‘Mother Nature’ in the end, though I did think about the name ‘Seasons’, as the fields are shown at different times over the farming year. Oh, okay. Do you think it's going to be challenging putting our displays together? Well, I've pretty much come to a conclusion about which pieces I'll include now. I'll have to miss out some of my preparatory drawings for the bigger pieces to make sure my best work fits into the space we've been allocated. I'm more concerned about how long it will take me to put everything in place. We've got a day and a half, that'll be plenty. We'll see. What about writing the summary of our work? It's for people who visit the exhibition to read, and I'm absolutely certain they will. It explains the reasons behind our work, and they'll want to know what it all means. We've got a strict word limit to stick to, but I've got so much to say, it won't be easy to say it in so few words. So what about other organizational stuff? We'll need good lighting for one thing. The technical guys are doing that, aren't they? Yeah. One thing to do is copy a load of comment forms so people can write what they think of the exhibition. Hopefully, they'll be kind. I'm sure they will. I don't know about the journalists who've been invited though, they might not be quite as nice to us. Well, fingers crossed. You never know. So our tutor suggested visiting a few exhibitions to look at the way work is presented and to give us a few ideas about improving and displaying our own work. Yeah, I like the On the Water exhibition. The way the artist used the brushstrokes in the oil painting to create a sense of movement was amazing. It takes a long time to develop skill like that. Maybe we'll get there one day. What I liked about the City Life exhibition was the fact that although the paintings themselves were of busy places, the display itself wasn't crowded at all. Perhaps the fact that the paintings were actually quite small was what created a more open feeling to the exhibition. Yeah, though the way they were arranged wasn't especially unusual. And then there was the Faces exhibition. Yeah, I mean, painting people's portraits isn't a new thing, but what I did like was the way the artist managed to reproduce the exact tones of the skin and hair of the people in the pictures. And the last exhibition we went to see was Moods. I expected that to show emotions, people laughing, crying, whatever, but it was about plants. You don't tend to think of trees and flowers having feelings... And I'm not sure they do, but it certainly seemed that way in the pictures. Not the most obvious choice of subject, that's for sure. Anyway, I guess we'd better get on with it.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Good morning. Today’s lecture is about the development of the telescope up until the end of the 17th century. We can trace the telescope’s earliest form back to the 1200s. History records Roger Bacon as possibly the first to invent a magnifying glass. The principal use of his invention was for reading. This proved to be a benefit mostly for researchers who, until then, had been forced to give up working while still relatively young because of impaired vision. In 1608, a Dutch astronomer called Lipperhey discovered that if convex and concave lenses were put together, they created a magnifying glass through which things at a distance could be seen. He created a miniature telescope. It was so small that, initially, people took it to the theater for a better view of the stage. Galileo found out about Lipperhey’s invention in the spring of 1609 and immediately set about improving it. Galileo experimented with different lenses, combining a weak convex lens with a strong concave lens. He discovered that this intensified the strength of the instrument. Unfortunately, the lenses the opticians were making for glasses were unsatisfactory for what Galileo wanted to do, as they did not have powerful enough magnification. Galileo, therefore, decided that to solve his problem, he would have to start the production of his own lenses. Eventually, he achieved a magnification about nine times more than you could see with the naked eye, an enormous improvement over everything else on the market. Galileo then decided to approach the Senate of Venice to demonstrate the improved instrument. Many senators were eager to try the new telescope and climbed the highest bell towers in Venice to look through the glass at ships far out to sea. The government of Venice was impressed by his invention’s obvious potential and envisioned the advantages this eyeglass could have for the army. His first major astronomical discovery with the telescope was that the moon’s surface was mountainous and not a perfect sphere, as it had always been assumed. During the lunar cycle of 28 days, he found that the shadow seemed to vary with the light. Galileo also figured out how to estimate the altitude of the mountains on the moon by looking for bright spots in the dark areas. Galileo looked for the spots when it was a half moon and, with geometry, was able to calculate the elevation of the mountains. From these calculations, he was able to draw charts of the terrain and show the altitudes of the mountains. In 1610, Galileo’s next major discovery was regarding Jupiter. Using a telescope with magnification 20 times the strength of his previous ones, he looked at Jupiter on successive nights. His main observation was a trio of what initially seemed to be small stars close to Jupiter. However, by the 15th night, he realized that they were going around the planet in a daily orbit and that, in fact, they were moons, not stars. Three days later, he saw a fourth one. This discovery showed how important a telescope was for astronomers. They would now be able to see celestial objects that could not previously be seen by the naked eye. In the late 1600s, scientists started to make a stronger telescope, revealing the galaxy. Scientists realized that when they increased the length of the telescope, the intensity of magnification improved significantly. One such telescope was created in 1656 and magnified over 100 times. It had an incredible length of 4 meters. Telescopes continued to become longer over the next few years, and, in fact, the astronomer Hevelius built one in 1670 that was 43 meters long. However, these telescopes were soon to prove useless for accurate observation because the slightest wind caused the instrument to shift. Finally, in 1675, astronomers abandoned the tube telescope and instead mounted the telescope on a building. Telescopes like this were called aerial telescopes. Scientists hoped that the stability of the mount would decrease the frustration when observing stars.

History records Roger Bacon as possibly the first to invent a magnifying glass. The principal use of his invention was for reading. This proved to be a benefit mostly for researchers who, until then, had been forced to give up working while still relatively young because of impaired vision. In 1608, a Dutch astronomer called Lipperhey discovered that if convex and concave lenses were put together, they created a magnifying glass through which things at a distance could be seen. He created a miniature telescope. It was so small that, initially, people took it to the theater for a better view of the stage. Galileo found out about Lipperhey’s invention in the spring of 1609 and immediately set about improving it. Galileo experimented with different lenses, combining a weak convex lens with a strong concave lens. He discovered that this intensified the strength of the instrument. Unfortunately, the lenses the opticians were making for glasses were unsatisfactory for what Galileo wanted to do, as they did not have powerful enough magnification. Galileo, therefore, decided that to solve his problem, he would have to start the production of his own lenses. Eventually, he achieved a magnification about nine times more than you could see with the naked eye, an enormous improvement over everything else on the market. Galileo then decided to approach the Senate of Venice to demonstrate the improved instrument. Many senators were eager to try the new telescope and climbed the highest bell towers in Venice to look through the glass at ships far out to sea. The government of Venice was impressed by his invention’s obvious potential and envisioned the advantages this eyeglass could have for the army. During the lunar cycle of 28 days, he found that the shadow seemed to vary with the light. Galileo also figured out how to estimate the altitude of the mountains on the moon by looking for bright spots in the dark areas. In the late 1600s, scientists started to make a stronger telescope, revealing the galaxy. Scientists realized that when they increased the length of the telescope, the intensity of magnification improved significantly. One such telescope was created in 1656 and magnified over 100 times. However, these telescopes were soon to prove useless for accurate observation because the slightest wind caused the instrument to shift. Finally, in 1675, astronomers abandoned the tube telescope and instead mounted the telescope on a building. Telescopes like this were called aerial telescopes. passages.title: Passage 1: Book review: Triumph of the City
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Book review: Triumph of the City

A. Triumph of the City, by Edward Glaeser, is a readable and often thrilling book. It is a hymn of praise to the city — an invention so important that we often take it for granted. Cities now shape global life. In 2018, 55 per cent of the world's population lived in urban areas. This figure is expected to reach 68 per cent by 2050. People continue to flood into cities to find jobs and opportunities. The crowds and poverty in some modern cities may horrify observers. However, the book does not present these conditions only as evidence of failure. It also sees them as signs of economic movement, growth and aspiration.

B. This view has faced more than two hundred years of resistance. The Industrial Revolution began in Britain. Soon after, the Romantic poets turned away from urban smoke and factories. They celebrated the air and light of untouched nature. In nineteenth-century America, Henry David Thoreau retreated to Walden Pond in 1845. He later published a book called Walden in 1854. In it, he described a solitary, simple life outside the city. His writing influenced generations of Americans. These readers came to associate cities with moral and physical decline. They regarded nature as a healthier alternative. However, the book sets this tradition beside the practical history of cities. The disadvantages of early urban life were real, but they were not permanent.

C. Early industrial cities were dirty. They lacked efficient waste-disposal systems. As a result, disease spread rapidly through crowded neighbourhoods. However, these cities were also profitable. This created strong commercial and political incentives to improve them. Paris is one of the clearest examples. Between 1853 and 1870, Napoleon III gave Baron Haussmann exceptionally unrestricted authority to reconstruct the city. Wide boulevards, sewers, parks and public spaces replaced many overcrowded and slum-infested districts. New York developed through a less centralised process. It began with the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. This plan imposed the Manhattan street grid on the city. The grid later supported large-scale commercial and residential growth. Both cities became major centres of ideas, trade and innovation.

D. The book also looks at the spectacle of urban poverty from an economic point of view. Poor people often flock to cities. Urban jobs give them a greater chance of becoming richer. Their labour also helps to reinvigorate the city economy. It is therefore folly to push them out through strict planning rules. Such rules limit new housing and cause property prices to soar. In some cities, jobs grow faster than the supply of homes. In these cities, poorer residents face the greatest difficulty in finding a place to live. Building more housing and improving infrastructure can make urban opportunities more accessible. In contrast, excessive restrictions place tremendous pressure on existing neighbourhoods and transport systems.

E. Problems arise when municipal authorities fail to balance preservation with growth. Paris is a good example. One of the city's great virtues is the historic character of Haussmann's nineteenth-century boulevards. The book defends the preservation of this central landscape. However, it questions the decision to put large-scale office development at La Défense. La Défense is on the western outskirts of Paris. The authority responsible for developing the district was set up in 1958. La Défense then grew into a major high-rise business centre outside the historic core. The book argues that commercial development around Montparnasse could have revitalised parts of central Paris instead. This would not have destroyed its architectural fabric. Some critics also argue that excessive preservation can turn historic centres into a living museum rather than a dynamic urban environment.

F. Mumbai shows a different problem. The issue is the link between building restrictions and outward expansion. The city's population grew from about 8.2 million in 1981 to about 12.5 million in the 2011 census. This growth happened within an area of roughly 603 square kilometres. As demand for homes and workplaces increased, restrictions were imposed on the height and volume of new buildings. This limited the usable space available in established urban locations. As a result, the city expanded into surrounding areas in an inefficient way. This sprawl also increased travel demands for many residents. The example supports the book's broader point. Dense cities cannot work well unless their planning systems allow enough housing and commercial space to be built where people need it.

G. In the United States, suburban expansion created another set of urban-planning problems. The book is repentant about the appeal of suburban life to families. It also recognises the legitimate financial pressures behind this choice. Petrol was relatively cheap. Planning rules raised inner-city property prices. As a result, moving to the suburbs became almost inevitable for many middle-class households. Suburbanites generally mingle less in dense public spaces. This reduces the face-to-face contact associated with urban creativity. Detached homes are also costlier to heat and cool than flats. Car-dependent households may drive around 15,000 miles a year. Greater household energy consumption and reliance on cars contribute to a larger carbon footprint. This strengthens the environmental case for compact cities.

passages.title: Passage 2: Ancient Storytelling
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Ancient Storytelling

A. The first stories were probably narrated to people crouching around a bonfire. These included tales of mighty adventures, like near-death encounters, hunting excursions, or an escape from mortal peril, or perhaps a mystery or divine anecdotes. However, irrespective of the subject, there was one principal objective behind all these tales: to keep the listener intrigued and engaged, to make them overlook their worries or fatigue, and only one query must prevail in their mind — what happens next?

B. Finding the initial stories ever told in human history is like herding cats, as these were preserved in the minds of the storytellers. This kind of storage or memorisation, however, shall not be deemed as ineffective. Several documented oral traditions of Australia, the Balkans, and other parts of the world apprise us of master storytellers and poets of the time that could recite thousands of verses and prose from their memory, word to word! However, while such memorisation seems like art or sorcery, the essential idea of creating symbols is to have a system of reminders or mnemonics that helps one recall specific information in one's mind.

C. In a few Polynesian societies, the storytellers used a notched memory stick for assistance in successive stages of recitation. However, among many other global communities, the art of storytelling led to the invention or development of writing systems. For instance, the onset of literacy in ancient Greece is attributed to the fact that the epic tales of the Trojan War and the Voyage of Odysseus were so captivating that there was a need to preserve them. Thus, the Greeks, in 750 B.C. — 700 B.C. borrowed the alphabet system from their Eastern Mediterranean neighbours, the Phoenicians.

D. The pristine practice of documenting stories on parchment and other materials can be traced to many ancient civilisations. The priestly papyrus archives of ancient Egypt and the birch-bark scrolls used by North American Ojibway Indians are excellent examples. It has emerged as a tried and tested practice, thanks to which stories are today synonymous with words on paper. Even the practice of oral storytelling is believed to have been taken over by journals, novels, comic strips, etc. However, written texts are not the primary source for humans to access stories. But then, what is it?

E. Each year, over seven billion people head towards the silver screens to watch the latest offerings of national and international cinema. Yes, the chief storyteller of the day is none other than the Cinema! The movies encompass storytelling in the form of motion pictures, which is a contemporary phenomenon in comparison to reading information on paper or still photography. It is more so an illusion that was originally accepted by the method of sequencing images in a particular order. Even so, it is imperative to acknowledge that the art of visual storytelling must hold a profoundly atavistic vibe to it. In spite of the advantage, the conventional patterns of storyline and characterisation that have been instilled in storytelling for ages are indispensable for a good story.

F. While thousands of scripts collect dust on the desks of major film studios, all an aspiring screenwriter needs to look up to is the fourth-century Greek philosopher, Aristotle. In his incomplete work, The Poetics, he left several lecture notes describing the art of storytelling in multiple literary and dramatic mediums. Though it is highly unlikely that he envisaged the popcorn-fuelled atmosphere of today's multiplexes, he had ample perception of how to gather and retain large crowds to such creative centres. Aristotle examined the process with impressive rationalism. He states that when a story fascinates us, we lose the sense of where we are, our fears, and accept fiction. This is one of Aristotle's principles of theatre, which he calls — 'the suspension of disbelief.'

G. The audience knows the feeling! They might have experienced episodes of horror, grief, astonishment or ecstasy, sitting on the theatre seats or even days after the show, knowing that it is all fiction yet letting it impact their state of mind. They seldom think through why they are caught in the web of the storyteller.

H. Aristotle taught at Athens, the city where theatre emerged as a prime mode of public leisure and entertainment. So it is evident that he might have observed suspended disbelief in action. Two theatrical storytelling types, tragedy and comedy, made Athenians immerse themselves in gloom and glee, respectively. Of which, Aristotle explicitly acknowledged tragedy as a potent weapon to trigger the most heartfelt emotions of the spectators, so he explored the factors in the storyteller's art that brought about such a subconscious commotion. For this, he studied the masterpieces of classical Greek tragedies by Euripides, Aeschylus, Sophocles, and even the epic poetry of Homer. Even at that time, Homer's stories commanded the same awe as today. His Iliad and the Odyssey were considered literary landmarks and used as a scale to measure all other stories.

I. So what is the mystery behind Homer's captivating narratives? Homer conceived credible heroes that were powerful and majestic but did not turn into fantasy figures in the end. He made them sulk, quarrel, cheat, and whine. These were the characteristics that an audience could relate to, or wish to follow. This naturally intrigued them to know what happens next. As Aristotle observed, the heroes with a human side, a mix of flaws and vulnerability to which humans are inclined, are aptly dramatic.

passages.title: Passage 3: Putting the brakes on climate change
passages.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

Putting the brakes on climate change

Are hydrogen cars the answer?

A. It is tempting to treat the survival of coral reefs and rainforests as a concern remote from traffic queues and polluted urban air, but it is not — scientists are now confident that rapid changes in the Earth's climate are already disrupting and altering many wildlife habitats, with pollution from vehicles forming a significant part of the problem. The ramifications are not restricted to distant ecosystems, since the same carbon-intensive transport paradigm that warms seas and changes rainfall patterns also exposes city dwellers to harmful air and makes decarbonisation politically urgent.

B. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that continued warming increases the likelihood of forest fires, drought-related dieback on land, and coral bleaching in increasingly warm oceans, while few species, if any, will remain immune to related changes in temperature, rainfall and sea level. In 2023, global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions reached about 37.4 gigatonnes, a scale that demonstrates why avoiding catastrophic disruption requires more than individual restraint: governments must slow deforestation while replacing coal, oil and gas, still the principal sources of energy in many economies, with credible alternatives.

C. Several technologies can reduce or eliminate carbon dioxide generated during daily energy consumption: wind and solar power have expanded rapidly, battery electric cars are becoming commonplace, and hydrogen fuel cells have re-entered public debate. Battery vehicles can be extremely efficient for ordinary journeys, yet charging times, mineral supply chains and access to charging in dense cities may pose practical limitations for some users; hydrogen advocates therefore argue that rapid refuelling and long range could be useful for buses, freight vehicles and other heavily used fleets. Fuel-cell technology was invented in the nineteenth century, but because the motor industry concentrated on refining the combustion engine for mass production, early designs did not become an established transport system.

D. In a modern fuel-cell car, whether a prototype or a commercially produced model, hydrogen is carried under pressure rather than stored solely in a large battery, while the vehicle resembles a conventional electric car in its quiet operation and responsive acceleration. Inside the cell, hydrogen combines electrochemically with oxygen to generate electricity for the motor, and the only tailpipe emission is water; unlike a battery, the cell does not run down while its supply of fuel continues. Systems of different sizes can power buses, backup generators or portable equipment, and fuel cells can achieve efficiencies of around 60 per cent, compared with approximately 20–30 per cent for a typical petrol-powered vehicle.

E. The apparent cleanliness of the exhaust, however, does not settle the question of lifecycle emissions, because hydrogen is an energy carrier rather than a freely available source of energy. Water is an abundant source from which industry can exploit hydrogen through electrolysis, yet, when the electricity required for that process comes from a coal- or gas-fired station, the supposed climate benefit can shrink dramatically. At present, renewable electricity is not always sufficiently cheap or continuously available for hydrogen to be manufactured on the immense scale required for road transport in an economically viable way, with recent estimates placing green hydrogen production at approximately US$2.8–6.4 per kilogram rather than the US$1 target sought for competitive deployment.

F. A transitional route uses natural gas, separating methane into its constituent components of hydrogen and carbon dioxide, with the latter captured and placed underground through so-called geological sequestration. Companies including Norway's Statoil, now Equinor, have stored carbon dioxide beneath the seabed, and supporters propose this approach as a supply route pending cheaper renewable hydrogen. Whether public finance should assist such an interim, gas-dependent option or accelerate fully renewable systems instead is ultimately a matter of policy priorities as well as technological feasibility.

G. Critics also challenge the thermodynamic feasibility of hydrogen cars when electricity could be deployed more directly in battery vehicles, since energy is lost in electrolysis, compression, distribution and its eventual reconversion inside the fuel cell. As one group of analysts puts it, “the energy required to produce, compress and distribute hydrogen makes the technology less efficient than direct electrification”, a criticism that does not make fuel cells useless but narrows the circumstances in which their energy return on investment may justify the infrastructural cost. Hydrogen may therefore be more persuasive for vehicles that travel long distances, return predictably to depots, or cannot afford lengthy charging stops than for small privately owned cars used mainly on urban journeys.

H. The market cannot solve that infrastructure problem simply by putting attractive vehicles in showrooms, because drivers will not buy cars without reliable stations and investors will not finance stations without assured demand. Although freak weather conditions have intensified pressure for action, a nationwide hydrogen infrastructure rollout would require coordinated standards, safe storage facilities and dependable fuel supplies; centrally managed bus fleets and courier vans offer a rational starting point because a limited number of depots can serve many vehicles each day. This pattern identifies why public transport adoption is not merely a publicity exercise but a practical first step in testing reliability and reducing risk before any large consumer market can emerge.

I. Policy makers, markets and engineers consequently face different, although connected, decisions: governments can fund research and set emissions standards, manufacturers in the automotive industry can improve durability and scalability, and purchasers can decide whether performance justifies cost. By 2024, more than 50 countries had published hydrogen strategies or road maps, yet policy ambition alone cannot guarantee technological readiness, affordable supply or low lifecycle emissions. Fuel-cell transport should therefore be treated neither as the sole solution nor as an expensive distraction: supported alongside renewable electricity, batteries and improved public transit, it could form one carefully targeted part of a long-term strategy for climate and wildlife protection.

task1.title: Task 1: Report / Data Description
task1.prompt: The chart and table below show the proportion of energy generated from renewable and non-renewable sources in selected OECD countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
task1.sampleBand8Answer:
The chart and accompanying table illustrate the comparative distribution of electricity production from renewable and conventional non-renewable sources across four OECD member nations—namely Germany, Sweden, Canada, and Japan—over a twenty-year timeframe from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, it is immediately apparent that all surveyed nations witnessed an upward trajectory in green energy adoption, with Sweden maintaining the foremost position in clean energy reliance throughout. Conversely, Japan continued to exhibit the lowest proportion of renewables despite moderate progress in the final decade.

In detail, Sweden commenced the period with 42% of its total energy coming from renewables in 2000, which subsequently expanded sharply to surpass 68% by 2020, driven primarily by investments in hydroelectric and wind installations. Canada similarly sustained high renewable dependency, starting at 56% and peaking at 64% by the end of the survey period.

In contrast, Germany underwent the most dramatic structural shift: renewable output represented a modest 8% in 2000 before quadrupling to approximately 39% in 2020 under comprehensive decarbonization initiatives. Japan, by comparison, began at just 7% and grew modestly to 18% in 2020, still leaving fossil and nuclear fuels to comprise the vast majority (82%) of its energy grid.

task2.title: Task 2: Academic Essay
task2.prompt: Some people believe that artificial intelligence and automation will bring massive unemployment and economic instability. Others argue that AI will foster innovation and create higher-value jobs. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
task2.sampleBand8Answer:
The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic automation has ignited rigorous debate across global economic forums. While a considerable segment of the population expresses trepidation regarding widespread redundancy and fiscal volatility, others contend that this technological paradigm will unlock unprecedented productivity and cultivate novel vocational sectors. In my view, although transient displacement is inevitable, AI will ultimately function as a net positive catalyst for societal affluence.

On the one hand, apprehensions regarding job scarcity are grounded in historical precedent and empirical reality. In routine-intensive fields such as manufacturing, logistics, and entry-level clerical administration, autonomous algorithms execute quantitative computations and physical tasks with far greater velocity and precision than human operators. Consequently, unmitigated deployment without rigorous retraining frameworks risks marginalizing millions of low-skilled workers, thereby exacerbating wealth disparity and burdening public welfare reserves.

On the other hand, proponents persuasively assert that technological upheavals historically eliminate specific tasks rather than labor as a whole. By relieving human professionals of mundane, repetitive drudgery, automation creates capacity for higher-order cognitive domains such as ethical AI governance, specialized software architecture, and creative strategic consulting. Furthermore, empirical analyses indicate that machine-augmented industries stimulate secondary employment ecosystems—from renewable infrastructure to tailored biotechnology—which generate premium remuneration.

In conclusion, while the transition phase undeniably poses formidable challenges for specific occupational demographics, artificial intelligence represents a profound evolution rather than an existential crisis for the labor market. Governments and educational institutions must proactively orchestrate lifelong upskilling programs to ensure equitable participation in this automated era.
